newsitem.title: BRAZIL: ING sees 3 pct Brazil growth in '97, 3.5 pct in'98.
newsitem.headline: ING sees 3 pct Brazil growth in '97, 3.5 pct in'98.

text.p: Brazil, unable to risk even modest growth without sparking huge external account deficits, will likely grow just three percent this year and 3.5 percent in 1998, ING Barings said.

"Authorities will prefer to keep the economy running at a slow pace of around three percent, which will not put pressure on the balance of payments," ING economist Jose Carlos de Faria said in a report.
But "eventually, the constraint on economic growth imposed by relatively flat exports and booming imports will have to be addressed," he added.

He forecast a trade deficit of $11.5 billion this year, with merchandise imports of $62 billion and exports of $50.5 billion, and a 1998 gap of $13.5 billion with $68.5 billion in imports and $55 billion in exports.
Last year, Brazil's Gross Domestic Product grew 2.91 percent and trade deficit reached $5.54 billion.

In May, Brazil's monthly trade deficit contracted to under $300 million from an average $1 billion monthly gap during 1997's first four months, with imports falling to $4.9 billion from $5.6 billion in April.

But "closer analysis shows that imports remained quite high in May compared with first-quarter 1997 or earlier periods and that it was the April imports which were excessive, even aberrant for this time of the year," Faria said.

Seasonally high exports account for May's improvement and will probably lead to a "reasonable" June trade figure but imports tend to rise in the second half of the year and exports will fall as harvests and shipments peak, he said.
"The trade deficit will probably be a recurring issue for the markets and the policymakers starting next month," he wrote.

Double-digit export growth such as that seen in Argentina, Mexico and Venezuela in the last few years would solve the problem of rising imports but recent Brazilian government efforts to boost sales abroad have been disappointing, he added.

Faria said the current "negative correlation" between growth and the trade balance began in 1995 and can be explained by the strong currency appreciation since the implementation of the Real Plan in July 1994 combined with liberalized trade rules.
The cornerstore of the anti-inflation Real Plan was the introduction of a strong and stable currency of the same name.

Faria said authorities are unlikely to devalue the Real significantly before October 1998 balloting when President Fernando Henrique Cardoso hopes to win re-election, he said. The real recently has only depreciated gradually under central bank guidance.

The real is currently trading at 1.07 to the dollar. Farias projected a year-end exchange rate of 1.11 reais to the dollar in 1997 and 1.20 reais next year, with inflation of eight and seven percent respectively.

Looking at economic prospects for this year and next, Faria said Brazil will opt for slow growth, "especially if the privatization process continues and keeps attracting direct and portfolio investment into Brazil."

However, "this growth rate is so low ... that it is likely to cause some political discomfort for the Cardoso administration, especially as it gears up to win re-election," Faria said. ((--James Craig, Sao Paulo newsroom 5511 2485413))
